title: Planning, Lesson 4: Scenarios and sensitivity - why a single number is the wrong answer
subtitle: Telling sensitivity from scenarios, choosing which variables to flex, and presenting a range to the leadership team
whyItMatters: Every plan is wrong; the useful question is how wrong it can be before it stops being survivable. A plan that produces exactly one number forces the decision-maker to either believe it or not, when what they actually need to know is the threshold at which they must change course.
openingQuestion: What is the difference between sensitivity analysis and scenario analysis?
openingOptions: Sensitivity is for the short term and scenarios for the long term
Sensitivity moves one variable, a scenario moves a whole group
Sensitivity uses past data, scenarios use forecast data
They are the same idea under two different names
explanation: Sensitivity answers the question of which variable matters most: hold everything else still, push one variable up and down, and see how far the result moves. A scenario answers something entirely different: what happens to us if a recession arrives - and in a recession revenue falls alongside margins falling and receivables slowing down. Pushing revenue down 20% on its own while holding the others fixed describes a world that does not exist.

diagram.label: Sensitivity: one variable, find the ones that matter
Scenario: a group of variables telling one story
Find the threshold that changes the decision
Present a range, not a point

realWorldExample.description: A plan to open 30 new stores produced a single profit figure, and the meeting turned into an argument about whether that figure could be believed. The rewrite presented three scenarios with their trigger conditions: in the base case, average revenue per store matches the current level; in the low case, revenue reaches only 80% and the payback period stretches from 14 months to 26. The decisive point was not the profit number but the finding attached to it: below 75%, the expansion swallows all the cash generated by the existing stores. The meeting shifted from believing or not believing to which indicator tells us which scenario we are in.

quiz.question: Why must a scenario change several variables at once?
options: Because moving several variables at once makes the result steadier
Because a model is only stable when at least three variables move
Because moving one variable alone describes a world that does not exist
Because the board usually asks to see every variable in the model move
quiz.explanation: In a recession, revenue does not fall on its own. Margins compress because prices have to come down, and customers pay more slowly - the three move together. None of the other answers describes a property of scenario analysis: moving more variables generally widens the spread of results rather than steadying it, models do not need a minimum number of moving inputs to work, and a board that asks for everything to move at once is asking for noise, not a story.

quiz.question: What is sensitivity analysis for, before you start building scenarios?
options: To cut the number of variables in the model to the bare minimum
To check whether the model contains a formula error in any cell
To pin down the single most accurate value for each variable in the plan
To find the few variables that matter most and build scenarios on them
quiz.explanation: Without this step, scenarios tend to get built around whichever variables came to mind first rather than the ones that actually drive the result. Sensitivity is a ranking exercise, not a cleanup exercise: it does not remove variables from the model, it does not audit formulas, and it certainly does not tell you the true value of any input - it only tells you which inputs are worth arguing about.

quiz.question: What is a break-point in scenario analysis?
options: The value of a variable at which the decision should change
The largest value a variable has reached in the whole history
The minimum profit the board has set as a target for the plan
The point where two different scenarios give the same result
quiz.explanation: This is the single most useful thing a scenario analysis produces. It turns the question of whether the plan is right into a far more concrete one: which indicator are we watching, and at what level do we change direction. A historical maximum is a data point, a profit target is an aspiration, and a crossing point between two scenarios is an arithmetic coincidence - none of them tells anyone what to do.

quiz.question: Why should you avoid presenting too many scenarios at once?
options: Because each added scenario makes the model take considerably longer to compute
Because decision-makers lose the comparison and fall back on the middle one
Because reporting standards cap how many options one document may set out
Because more scenarios lower the odds that the base case actually happens
quiz.explanation: Three scenarios is the common number because it is just enough to show a range while still being memorable. Seven scenarios feel thorough but in practice return the discussion to exactly where it started. Computation time is irrelevant on any modern spreadsheet, no reporting standard limits the count, and adding scenarios does not change the probability of the base case - it only changes how many things the reader has to hold in mind.

quiz.question: Why should you avoid putting too many scenarios in front of the leadership team at once?
options: Because low-probability scenarios never actually happen in practice
Because each scenario needs its own model and takes time to build
Because too much choice dilutes the decision instead of aiding
Because the spreadsheet can only display three scenarios at once
quiz.explanation: Three scenarios force the audience to confront the range and prepare an action for each branch. With seven, everyone picks the one that suits the belief they already held, and the meeting returns to exactly where it began. A low-probability scenario can and sometimes does occur - that is why it is modelled at all - and neither build time nor any software limit is the reason to keep the count down.

keyTakeaways: Sensitivity moves one variable to find the ones that matter; a scenario moves a whole group along one consistent story
Run sensitivity first so you know which variables to build the scenarios around
The most valuable output is the break-point: at what level does the decision change
Three scenarios is enough - beyond that the audience falls back on looking only at the middle one

practicePrompt.question: The leadership team asks: is this plan achievable? What is the most useful way to answer?
options: Yes, based on the current set of assumptions
Yes if conversion stays above 3.2%; below that we miss by 15%
No one can answer for certain, because the future is unknowable
Yes, with a probability of roughly 70%
practicePrompt.explanation: This answer moves the discussion from belief to a trackable indicator with a specific action attached to a threshold. A 70% probability sounds quantitative but says nothing about where the figure came from and leads to nothing anyone has to do about it.

summary.keyIdea: Present a range of outcomes with the threshold that changes the decision, rather than one number
summary.commonMistake: Calling it a scenario while only moving revenue, leaving margins and receivables untouched
summary.action: In your current plan, find one variable where a bad enough move would make you recommend changing direction.

application.title: What to do
application.message: Run sensitivity on the five largest inputs to find the two with the strongest effect on the result. Then build exactly three scenarios around those two, and for each one write down the signal that tells you that is the scenario you are in.
application.secondary: The signal matters more than the number itself: without it, a scenario is only an exercise.

sections.text: A plan that produces exactly one number leaves the decision-maker with nothing to do but believe it or not. What they need is a different question answered: how far off do we have to be before we act differently.

sections.title: Sensitivity, scenarios and break-points
sections.subtitle: Three things whose names get mixed up constantly, answering three completely different questions

concepts.def: Move one variable, hold the rest. Answers: which variable matters most, what is the result sensitive to. It is the screening step that comes first.
Move a whole group of variables along one consistent story. Answers: if a recession arrives, what happens to us.
The value at which the decision has to change. This is the most useful output, because it turns the analysis into an indicator worth tracking.

sections.label: A scenario has to be internally consistent
sections.text: The most common mistake is calling something a downside scenario while only cutting revenue by 20%, leaving margins, days sales outstanding and the cost of capital untouched. In reality those move together: falling revenue usually brings discounting, slower payment, and a stricter bank. A scenario is only useful when it describes a world that could actually exist.
Why a 20% fall in revenue cuts profit by 80%

Revenue 100, variable costs 60, fixed costs 30, profit 10. The downside scenario cuts revenue to 80: variable costs fall to 48, but fixed costs are still 30, so profit is 2. Revenue down 20%, profit down 80%. That is operating leverage, and it is why a sensitivity table showing only percentage changes in revenue hides the most important part - the reader extrapolates linearly and reaches the wrong conclusion about how dangerous the situation is.

sections.label: A scenario has to be internally consistent
sections.text: The most common mistake is calling something a downside scenario while only cutting revenue by 20% and holding every other assumption fixed. A real scenario has to ask: if revenue falls because demand is weak, can we hold price, does the collection period stretch, does inventory build up, do we have to freeze hiring? These variables move together because they share a cause - and a scenario that ignores that produces a more comfortable number than reality at exactly the moment the truth matters most.

left.label: Sensitivity - move one variable
left.text: Hold everything else, change one assumption, see how far the result shifts. The purpose is RANKING: which variable deserves the time it takes to estimate it properly. If changing the churn assumption swings the result 40% while changing the office cost assumption swings it 1%, you know which one to argue about.

right.label: Scenario - move a whole cluster at once
right.text: Build one consistent story about the world and let every assumption move with it. The purpose is PREPARATION: if this happens, how many months of cash are left, and at what point must we act. The useful output is not a number but a trigger level.

lines: Nobody blames you for missing a plan. They blame you when nobody knew it was being missed until it was too late.
The next lesson goes into the biggest source of internal argument around any management report: whose cost is it.
